title: DNA variants detected in primary and metastatic lung adenocarcinoma: a case report and review of the literature
author: Christina Kelly; Caitlin Raymond; Song Han; Youmin Lin; Linyijia Chen; Gengming Huang; Jianli Dong
text:
Abstract
Non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has been found to have recurrent genetic abnormalities, and novel therapies targeting these aberrations have improved patient survival. In this study, specimens from benign tissue, primary tumors, and brain metastases were obtained at autopsy from a 55-year-old White female patient diagnosed with NSCLC and were examined using next-generation sequencing (NGS) and chromosomal microarray assay (CMA). No genetic aberrations were noted in the benign tissue; however, NGS identified a mutation in the KRAS proto-oncogene, GTPase (KRAS): KRAS exon 2 p.G12D in primary and metastatic tumor specimens. We observed 7 DNA copy number aberrations (CNAs) in primary and metastatic tumor specimens; an additional 7 CNAs were exclusively detected in the metastatic tumor specimens. These DNA alterations may be genetic drivers in the pathogenesis of the tumor specimen from our patient and may serve as biomarkers for the classification and prognosis of NSCLC.
Keywords: non–small cell lung cancer, oncogenic driver, chromosome microarray, DNA copy number abnormality, next-generation sequencing, gene mutation
Introduction
Lung cancer is the second-most-common malignant neoplasm in the United States, preceded only by prostate cancer in men and breast cancer in women.1 Lung cancer is the leading cause of death from cancer. The American Cancer Society estimates 238,340 new cases and 127,070 deaths from lung and bronchial cancer in the United States during the year 2023.1 These numbers represent 12.2% of all new cancer cases and 20.8% of all cancer deaths predicted. To put these figures into perspective, approximately 350 people die of lung cancer daily in the United States. Moreover, the 5-year survival rate of lung and bronchial cancer averaged only 23% in the years 2012 through 2018.1
There are 2 types of lung cancer: non–small cell carcinoma (NSCLC) and small cell carcinoma (SCC). The most common type of NSCLC is adenocarcinoma, which is derived from glandular tissue and often originates in the periphery of the lung.2 Although smoking elevates the risk of lung adenocarcinoma, a notable proportion of patients with that type of cancer are nonsmokers. In addition to smoking tobacco, family history of lung cancer and occupational exposure are also associated with the development of lung adenocarcinoma. The disease typically progresses from atypical adenomatous hyperplasia to adenocarcinoma in situ, which then progresses to minimally invasive adenocarcinoma and ultimately to invasive adenocarcinoma.2 Clinically, lung adenocarcinoma may remain asymptomatic in early stages but can present with symptoms such as weight loss, cough, shortness of breath, and other nonspecific presentations in late stages.2
Recurrent genetic and genomic abnormalities have been identified in NSCLC that may have diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive value.3,4 In this report, we present a case study of a 55-year-old White woman who died from NSCLC. Via next-generation sequencing (NGS) and chromosomal microarray (CMA), we found hot-spot KRAS exon 2 p.G12D mutation and 7 DNA copy-number aberrations (CNAs) in primary and metastatic tumor specimens, along with 7 CNAs exclusive to the metastatic tumor specimen.
Patient History
The patient, who had no known previous disease, presented with acute severe leg and back pain. Her surgical history consisted of a right breast tumor that was presumed benign. Her social history included a smoking history of 35 packs of cigarettes per year. Her sister (who had died at age 51) and mother had experienced unspecified lung cancer.
After her symptoms had worsened for 2 weeks, the patient underwent spinal MRI, which revealed extensive lesions that were concerning for metastases. A pathologic fracture at the eleventh thoracic vertebra (T11) was noted, with a pending pathologic fracture in the right femur. The patient was admitted to the hospital for workup and further imaging. Computed tomographic scan of her thorax showed mass-like consolidation in the left lower lobe with adjacent satellite nodularity and interlobular septal thickening, as well as multiple pulmonary nodules in the right lower lobe and enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes. Brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated multifocal metastatic disease of the calvarium, infundibular masses, and a clival lesion. Computed tomography–guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of the mass on the left lower lobe of the lung showed malignant cells in sheets with honeycomb pattern overlying a background of mucin. The cells possessed moderately vacuolated cytoplasm with round to oval pleomorphic hyperchromatic nuclei and prominent nucleoli, and tested positive for thyroid transcription factor–1 (TTF-1), cytokeratin 7 (CK7), caudal type homeobox 2 (CDX2), and cytokeratin 20 (CK20).
The patient was diagnosed with adenocarcinoma consistent with primary lung adenocarcinoma. Due to the pending pathologic fracture of the right hip, a decision to pursue right hip arthroplasty was made. However, the patient experienced gastric perforation 1 day after arthroplasty and developed rapid-onset oxygen desaturation associated with a drop in pulse and blood pressure that resulted in asystole and death. She had received no cancer treatment before her death. The findings at autopsy were consistent with metastatic adenocarcinoma, with the immediate cause of death being massive peritonitis from gastric perforation.
Formalin-fixed and paraffin-embedded (FFPE) specimens of primary lung tumor and metastatic tumor tissue from the brain of the patient, along with a fresh healthy cardiac muscle specimen, were obtained at the autopsy, which was performed 4 days after death. Genomic DNA and RNA were extracted and purified using AllPrep DNA/RNA Kits (QIAGEN). AmpliSeq for Illumina Focus Panel NGS assay was performed using the Illumina MiSeqDx instrument according to manufacturer instructions (Illumina). The AmpliSeq for Illumina Focus Panel is a targeted resequencing assay for biomarker analysis of 52 genes with known relevance to solid tumors including epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), KRAS, b-raf proto-oncogene, serine/threonine kinase (BRAF), erb-b2 receptor tyrosine kinase 2 (ERBB2), ALK receptor tyrosine kinase (ALK), ROS proto-oncogene 1, receptor tyrosine kinase (ROS1), ret proto-oncogene (RET), mitogen-activated protein kinase kinase (MEK), neurotrophic receptor tyrosine kinase 1 (NTRK1), NTRK2, and NTRK3 routinely analyzed in the clinical management of NSCLC. A KRAS exon 2 p.G12D mutation was detected in the primary and metastatic tumor specimens but not in the benign tissue. Given the positive family history of lung cancer, the fresh normal cardiac muscle specimen was examined via whole-exome sequencing using SSELXT HS Human All Exon V8+NCV Kit (Agilent Technologies) on an Illumina NextSeq 550Dx instrument (Illumina). However, no variants of significance were identified.
CMA was performed using OncoScan microarray according to manufacturer instructions (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The OncoScan microarray consists of more than 220,000 probes that can detect DNA copy number alterations including gains, losses, and copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH). Results were investigated using the Chromosome Analysis Suite (ChAS; Thermo Fisher Scientific). The settings for the smallest copy number variation (CNV) regions in the ChAS were 50 Kb and 50 markers for gains, 25 Kb and 25 markers for losses, and 5 Mb for CN-LOH. CMA results for specimens from our patient revealed copy number gain at 1q21.1q44 and copy number losses of chromosomes 1p31.3p11.2, 6q, 9p, 19, and 22q in the primary and metastatic tumor specimens (FIGURE 1, TABLE 1). These changes were not observed in the benign tissue from the patient, suggesting the somatic origin of the changes. Also, CNAs unique to the metastatic tumor specimen included copy number gains of chromosomes 8p12q24.3, 11q13.2q23.2, 12, and 15q22.2q26.3, as well as copy number losses of chromosomes 8p23.3p12, 9q22.32q34.11, and 11q23.2q25 (FIGURE 1, TABLE 1), suggesting their involvement in the metastatic process of tumor cells.

Discussion
In this study report, we present DNA abnormalities detected in primary and metastatic tumor specimens in a 55-year-old White female patient diagnosed with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma. We identified KRAS exon 2 p.G12D mutations in primary and metastatic tumor specimens, as well as copy number gains at chromosome 1q21.1q44 and copy number losses at chromosomes 1p31.3p11.2, 6q, 9p, 19, and 22q. The absence of these genetic aberrations in benign tissue suggests their somatic occurrence, and their presence in primary and metastatic specimens suggests that they act as drivers involved in tumor initiation or maintenance. Copy number gains at chromosome 8p12q24.3, 11q13.2 q23.2, 12, and 15q22.2q26.3 and copy number losses at chromosome 8p23.3p12, 9q22.32q34.11, and 11q23.2q25 were detected solely in the metastatic tumor specimen, indicating positive selection operating later in tumor progression and metastasis.
KRAS mutations occur in as many as 33% of NSCLC specimens and have been linked to White ethnicity, female sex, adenocarcinoma histology, and positive smoking history.3,11 It has been reported12 that KRAS mutations were more frequent in primary lung adenomas that metastasized to the brain (32/55 [58%]), as was the case with our patient.
KRAS is located at chromosome 12p12.1 (OMIM 190070) and encodes a GTPase that is inactive when bound to GDP and active when bound to GTP. Most KRAS mutations constitutively activate the KRAS protein by promoting its GTP-bound form, resulting in dysregulation of the intracellular signaling pathways involved in malignant transformation, tumor progression, and metastasis. Most KRAS mutations in NSCLC occur in exons 2-4. Codon 12 of the KRAS gene is the most common site of mutation in NSCLC and normally encodes glycine. Any mutation that changes glycine to an amino acid other than proline will induce steric hindrance and impair conversion of KRAS from its active GTP-bound form to its inactive GDP-bound form. The KRAS exon 2 p.G12D mutation identified in this case specifically replaces amino acid glycine with aspartic acid, which introduces steric hindrance and favors the active form KRAS. There are ongoing clinical and preclinical studies targeting KRAS mutations—including exon 2 p.G12D—in the treatment of NSCLC.11
Several previous studies have been conducted to identify distinct CNAs associated with adenocarcinoma vs squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) in NSCLC.6,7,10 Losses of 6q, 19, and 22q, found in primary tumor specimens in our patient, were specifically identified in lung adenocarcinoma but not in lung SCC. Whether these CNAs are useful biomarkers in the subclassification of NSCLC warrants further attention.
Three CNAs identified in this study, gains of 8p12q24.3 and 11q13.2 q23.2 and loss of 9p, harbor MYC proto-oncogene (MYC, 8q24.21, OMIM 190080), yes1-associated transcriptional regulator (YAP1, 11q22.1, OMIM 606608), matrix metallopeptidase 13 (MMP13, 11q22.2, OMIM 600108), and cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor 2A/B (CDKN2A/B, 9p21.3, OMIM 600160/600431), respectively. These genes were previously identified as drivers of metastasis of lung adenocarcinoma.13
In our patient, we were intrigued to find that, consistent with the results of a previous study,13 gains of 8p12q24.3 and 11q13.2 q23.2 were only identified in the metastatic specimen, whereas loss of 9p was found in primary and metastatic specimens. Whether these CNVs were associated with significant changes in the expression of these genes is unknown. Note that there were 3 copies of MYC (1 copy gain) and 4 copies of YAP1 and MMP13 (2 copy gain), and 1 copy of CDKN2A/B (1 copy loss) in the tumor specimens. Further studies are required to determine whether amplification of MYC/YAP1/MMP13 (eg, a total of >6 copies) and homozygous loss of CDKN2A/B are associated with tumor metastasis.
KRAS gene mutations are associated with a poor prognosis, with exon 2 p.G12D mutations being particularly correlated with poor overall survival.14 However, current therapies are in development that selectively target the KRAS exon 2 p.G12D allele and hold promise for improving treatment.15 Also, recurrent CNAs in NSCLC may be used to predict prognosis. For example, amplifications of 12p12.1 and 12p13.33 are associated with worse prognosis in NSCLC.16
The results of this study are consistent with the high frequency of KRAS mutation and extensive CNAs in lung adenocarcinoma. The findings in benign tissue, primary tumor specimens, and metastatic tumor specimens support the clonal evolution of tumor progression and metastasis driven by genetic aberrations. This study report contributes to further investigation in the literature of clinically useful genetic and genomic biomarkers in the diagnosis, classification, and prognosis of, and targeted therapy for, NSCLC.
